```{r}
#| include: false
source("assets/setup.R")
source("assets/quiz.R")
cc <- ncd |> drop_na(htn, salt_g, age, bmi, waist, sex, residence, education, tobacco, alcohol, phys_act)
m_crude <- glm(htn ~ salt_g, data = cc, family = binomial)
m_adj   <- glm(htn ~ salt_g + age + bmi + sex + residence + education + tobacco + alcohol + phys_act,
               data = cc, family = binomial)
b_salt  <- coef(m_adj)[["salt_g"]]
prev    <- mean(ncd$htn)
```

## Where we are

::: {.incremental}
- Sessions 2–4: **continuous** outcome → linear regression
- Today: **binary** outcome (hypertension yes/no) → **logistic regression**
- By the end you can:
  - explain **odds, log-odds** and **why we exponentiate** β into an OR
  - build crude and adjusted ORs with CIs
  - compare models by **likelihood ratio test** and **AIC**; read **pseudo-R²** honestly
  - judge **calibration** and **discrimination** (Hosmer–Lemeshow, ROC/AUC)
  - know when the **OR overstates** the prevalence ratio
:::

# A binary outcome {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Hypertension in our survey

```{r}
ncd |> count(htn_f) |> mutate(percent = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1))
```

::: {.fragment}
**`r round(100 * prev)`%** of adults are hypertensive — a **common** outcome. (Remember this for the OR vs PR discussion.)
:::

## Why not just use linear regression?

```{r}
lpm <- lm(htn ~ age + salt_g + bmi + sex, data = cc)     # "linear probability model"
range(fitted(lpm))
sum(fitted(lpm) < 0)                                      # people with a negative "probability"
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {.bad}
Fit a straight line to a 0/1 outcome and some people get a **negative "probability"**.
:::
:::

## A straight line leaves the 0–1 range

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.2
tibble(age = 15:90) |>
  mutate(p = predict(lm(htn ~ age, cc), pick(age))) |>
  ggplot(aes(age, p)) +
  geom_line(colour = col_red, linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0, 1), linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-.5, 1.5)) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "'Probability' of hypertension")
```

## Three problems with a straight line for a 0/1 outcome

| Problem | Why |
|---|---|
| **Impossible predictions** | A line is unbounded: probabilities fall below 0 or above 1 |
| **Non-constant variance** | The variance of a 0/1 outcome is p(1 − p): it depends on the mean |
| **Non-normal errors** | Residuals can only take two values per fitted value |

::: {.fragment}
::: {.key}
**Idea:** model a *transformation* of the probability that **can** take any value from −∞ to +∞ — the **log-odds**.
:::
:::

# Probability → odds → log-odds {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Three ways to express the same risk

::: {.eq .small}
odds = p ÷ (1 − p)

log-odds = ln(odds) = ln [ p ÷ (1 − p) ]
:::

```{r}
tibble(probability = c(.10, .25, .32, .50, .75, .90)) |>
  mutate(odds = round(probability / (1 - probability), 2),
         `log-odds` = round(log(odds), 2))
```

::: {.fragment}
**Worked example:** our prevalence is 32% → odds = 0.32 ÷ 0.68 = **0.47** ("about 1 hypertensive for every 2 non-hypertensive") → log-odds = ln 0.47 = **−0.75**.
:::

## The logit scale is unbounded and symmetric

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.3
tibble(logodds = seq(-6, 6, .05)) |>
  mutate(p = plogis(logodds)) |>
  ggplot(aes(logodds, p)) +
  geom_line(colour = col_red, linewidth = 1.4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0, 1), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("text", x = .2, y = .15, hjust = 0, label = "log-odds 0 = odds 1\n= probability 50%", size = 5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "log-odds (can be any number)", y = "probability (always 0–100%)")
```

## A 2×2 example: age and hypertension

```{r}
tab <- ncd |> count(age50, htn_f) |> pivot_wider(names_from = htn_f, values_from = n)
tab <- tab |> mutate(risk = round(HTN / (HTN + `No HTN`), 3), odds = round(HTN / `No HTN`, 3))
tab
c(OR = tab$odds[2] / tab$odds[1], PR = tab$risk[2] / tab$risk[1]) |> round(2)
```

::: {.fragment}
Among **50+** the odds are **`r tab$odds[2]`**, among **<50** **`r tab$odds[1]`**: **OR = `r round(tab$odds[2]/tab$odds[1], 1)`**. The prevalence ratio is only **`r round(tab$risk[2]/tab$risk[1], 1)`**. Keep this gap in mind.
:::

# The model {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## The logistic regression equation

::: {.eq}
logit(p) = ln [ p ÷ (1 − p) ] = β~0~ + β~1~x~1~ + β~2~x~2~ + …
:::

::: {.incremental}
- The **right side** is just like linear regression
- The **left side** is the **log-odds** of the outcome
- Solve for the probability: **p = 1 ÷ (1 + exp[ −(β~0~ + β~1~x~1~ + …) ])** — always between 0 and 1
- Coefficients are estimated by **maximum likelihood**, not least squares
:::

## Fitting it: `glm(family = binomial)`

```{r}
m_crude <- glm(htn ~ salt_g, data = cc, family = binomial)
summary(m_crude)$coefficients |> round(3)
```

::: {.fragment}
β for salt = **`r round(coef(m_crude)[["salt_g"]], 2)`** — a change in **log-odds** per g/day. Not yet something a clinician can use: next we convert it.
:::

## The S-shaped curve

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.2
ggplot(cc, aes(salt_g, htn)) +
  geom_jitter(height = .03, alpha = .25, colour = col_blue) +
  geom_smooth(method = "glm", method.args = list(family = binomial), colour = col_red, formula = y ~ x) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Salt intake (g/day)", y = "Probability of hypertension")
```

# Why we exponentiate β {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Step 1 — the model speaks in log-odds

::: {.eq}
ln [ odds(x) ] = β~0~ + β~1~ x
:::

β~1~ is the change in **log-odds** for a **one-unit** increase in x. We want a **ratio of odds**, so compare the model at **x + 1** and at **x**.

## Step 2 — compare x + 1 with x

::: {.eq .small}
ln [ odds(x + 1) ] = β~0~ + β~1~ (x + 1) = β~0~ + β~1~x + β~1~
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.eq .small}
ln [ odds(x + 1) ] − ln [ odds(x) ] = (β~0~ + β~1~x + β~1~) − (β~0~ + β~1~x) = **β~1~**
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.eq .small}
ln [ odds(x + 1) ÷ odds(x) ] = β~1~
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.eq}
OR = odds(x + 1) ÷ odds(x) = **e^β~1~^**
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
The β0 and the x terms cancel: that is why the OR for a one-unit change does not depend on the starting value of x, nor on the other covariates (they cancel as well). A difference in logs is the log of a ratio; exponentiate both sides to undo the log.
:::

## Step 3 — a worked number from our model

```{r}
b_salt <- coef(m_adj)[["salt_g"]]
c(beta = b_salt, OR_per_1g = exp(b_salt), OR_per_5g = exp(5 * b_salt), same_as = exp(b_salt)^5) |> round(3)
```

::: {.incremental}
- β = **`r round(b_salt, 3)`** → **OR per g/day = e^`r round(b_salt, 3)` = `r round(exp(b_salt), 2)`**
- Per **5 g/day**: e^(5 × β) = `r round(exp(5*b_salt), 2)` — ORs **multiply**, they do not add
- "Each extra 1 g/day multiplies the **odds** of hypertension by **`r round(exp(b_salt), 2)`**, holding the other variables constant"
:::

## Check it directly with two different people

```{r}
profile <- tibble(age = c(35, 35, 62, 62), sex = factor(c("Female", "Female", "Male", "Male"), levels(cc$sex)),
                  salt_g = c(8, 9, 8, 9), bmi = c(22, 22, 29, 29),
                  residence = factor("Rural", levels(cc$residence)), education = factor("Primary", levels(cc$education)),
                  tobacco = factor("No", levels(cc$tobacco)), alcohol = factor("No", levels(cc$alcohol)),
                  phys_act = factor("low", levels(cc$phys_act)))
p <- predict(m_adj, profile, type = "response"); odds <- p / (1 - p)
c(young_woman = odds[2] / odds[1], older_man = odds[4] / odds[3]) |> round(3)
```

::: {.fragment}
Whatever the person's other characteristics, 8 → 9 g/day multiplies the odds by **exactly e^β = `r round(exp(b_salt), 3)`**. The **probability** change differs by person; the **OR does not**.
:::

## Confidence intervals: exponentiate the limits too

```{r}
ci_log <- confint(m_adj)["salt_g", ]                       # profile-likelihood CI on the log-odds scale
rbind(`log-odds (β)` = c(est = b_salt, ci_log), `odds ratio` = exp(c(est = b_salt, ci_log))) |> round(3)
```

::: {.incremental}
- CI for β is built on the **log scale**, where it is (approximately) symmetric
- Exponentiating each limit gives the CI for the OR: **`r round(exp(b_salt), 2)` (`r round(exp(ci_log[1]), 2)` to `r round(exp(ci_log[2]), 2)`)**
- Because *exp* stretches the right side more, the **OR CI is asymmetric** around the estimate
:::

## Symmetric on the β scale, asymmetric on the OR scale

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
bind_rows(
  tidy(m_adj, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = .95) |> mutate(scale = "log-odds (β)"),
  tidy(m_adj, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) |> mutate(scale = "odds ratio (OR)")) |>
  filter(term %in% c("sexMale", "alcoholYes", "salt_g")) |>
  mutate(scale = fct_inorder(scale), null = if_else(scale == "odds ratio (OR)", 1, 0)) |>
  ggplot(aes(estimate, term)) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = null), linetype = "dashed", colour = col_red) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high), colour = col_navy) +
  facet_wrap(~ scale, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, caption = "Dashed line = no effect: β = 0 on the left, OR = 1 on the right")
```

## Why OR = 1 corresponds to β = 0

::: {.eq}
e^0^ = 1  ⇒  β = 0  ⇔  OR = 1
:::

::: {.incremental}
- OR = 1 means **no change in the odds** — no association
- A CI for the OR that **includes 1** is the same as a CI for β that **includes 0** → not significant at 5%
- OR **> 1** = higher odds; OR **< 1** = lower odds (**β > 0 / β < 0**)
:::

## Crude vs adjusted ORs

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
t_crude <- cc |> select(htn, salt_g, age, bmi, sex, residence, education, tobacco, alcohol, phys_act) |>
  tbl_uvregression(method = glm, y = htn, method.args = list(family = binomial), exponentiate = TRUE)
t_adj <- tbl_regression(m_adj, exponentiate = TRUE)
tbl_merge(list(t_crude, t_adj), tab_spanner = c("**Crude**", "**Adjusted**"))
```

::: {.notes}
Compare crude and adjusted: salt 1.46 → 1.24; education gradient disappears; physical activity appears only after adjustment (high activity OR about 0.57) — a first warning against screening variables by crude p-value (Session 6).
:::

## Reading an OR, its CI and its p-value

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.key}
**Salt:** adjusted OR **`r round(exp(b_salt), 2)`** (95% CI `r round(exp(ci_log[1]), 2)`–`r round(exp(ci_log[2]), 2)`), p < 0.001
:::

::: {.incremental}
- **Direction:** OR > 1 → higher odds with more salt
- **Size:** 24% higher odds per g/day; ≈ 3× per 5 g/day
- **Precision:** CI excludes 1
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.key}
**Sex:** adjusted OR **`r round(exp(coef(m_adj)[["sexMale"]]), 1)`** for men vs women (reference)
:::

::: {.warn}
An OR is a ratio of **odds**, not a ratio of **risks**. For a common outcome, "twice the odds" is **not** "twice as likely" (see later).
:::
:::
:::

# Likelihood-based assessment {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Likelihood: how probable were the data we saw?

```{r}
p_hat <- c(0.8, 0.3, 0.2)       # model's predicted P(hypertension) for 3 people
y     <- c(1,   0,   0)         # what actually happened
per_person <- ifelse(y == 1, p_hat, 1 - p_hat)
per_person
c(likelihood = prod(per_person), log_likelihood = sum(log(per_person)), deviance = -2 * sum(log(per_person))) |> round(3)
```

::: {.incremental}
- **Likelihood** = product of the probabilities the model gave to what really happened
- **Log-likelihood** = its logarithm (easier arithmetic; always ≤ 0; **closer to 0 = better fit**)
- **Deviance** = −2 × log-likelihood (relative to a perfect model): **smaller = better fit**
:::

## Maximum likelihood: the peak of the curve

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
bhat <- coef(m_crude)[["salt_g"]]
prof <- tibble(b = seq(bhat - .3, bhat + .3, length.out = 100)) |>
  mutate(ll = map_dbl(b, \(b) as.numeric(logLik(glm(htn ~ 1 + offset(b * salt_g), data = cc, family = binomial)))))
ci <- confint(m_crude)["salt_g", ]

ggplot(prof, aes(b, ll)) +
  geom_line(colour = col_navy, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = max(prof$ll) - qchisq(.95, 1) / 2, linetype = "dashed", colour = col_red) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(bhat, ci), linetype = c("solid", "dotted", "dotted"), colour = col_blue) +
  labs(x = "candidate β for salt (log-odds per g/day)", y = "log-likelihood",
       caption = "Peak = maximum-likelihood estimate · red line = 1.92 below the peak → the 95% CI")
```

::: {.notes}
Each point on the curve is the log-likelihood if the true salt β were that value (intercept re-optimised). The estimate sits at the peak. Values whose log-likelihood is within 1.92 of the peak (half of the chi-square 3.84 cut-off) form the likelihood-based 95% CI — this is what `confint()` uses.
:::

## Deviance and log-likelihood in R

```{r}
tibble(model = c("intercept only", "salt only", "adjusted"),
       logLik   = c(logLik(glm(htn ~ 1, binomial, cc)), logLik(m_crude), logLik(m_adj)),
       deviance = c(deviance(glm(htn ~ 1, binomial, cc)), deviance(m_crude), deviance(m_adj)),
       params   = c(1, 2, length(coef(m_adj)))) |> mutate(across(c(logLik, deviance), ~ round(.x, 1)))
```

::: {.fragment}
More predictors → higher log-likelihood and **lower deviance**. The question is whether the improvement is **more than chance** — that is the likelihood ratio test.
:::

## Likelihood ratio test (LRT) for nested models {.smaller}

::: {.key}
**H₀:** the extra coefficients are all zero.  **Test statistic = 2 × (logLik~big~ − logLik~small~)** ~ χ² with df = number of extra parameters.
:::

```{r}
m_small <- glm(htn ~ age + sex, data = cc, family = binomial)
m_big   <- glm(htn ~ age + sex + salt_g + bmi + tobacco + alcohol + phys_act, data = cc, family = binomial)
anova(m_small, m_big, test = "LRT")
lmtest::lrtest(m_small, m_big)
```

## Why LRT rather than Wald for comparing models

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.incremental}
- **Multi-df terms**: education has 3 dummies — Wald gives 3 separate p-values; the LRT asks **"does education matter at all?"** once
- **Small samples / big effects**: Wald can be unreliable (Hauck–Donner)
- LRT is **invariant to re-parameterisation**; Wald is not
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
drop1(m_adj, test = "LRT") |> as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("term") |> select(term, Df, AIC, LRT, `Pr(>Chi)`) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ signif(.x, 3)))
```
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
drop1 refits the model without each term: one LRT per term including the 3-df education and 2-df physical activity terms.
:::

## AIC: comparing models that are not nested

```{r}
m_bmi   <- glm(htn ~ age + sex + bmi,   data = cc, family = binomial)
m_waist <- glm(htn ~ age + sex + waist, data = cc, family = binomial)
AIC(m_bmi, m_waist)
```

::: {.incremental}
- **AIC = −2 log-likelihood + 2 × (number of parameters)** — fit, penalised for complexity
- **Lower is better**; a difference **< 2** means essentially no preference
- Works for **non-nested** comparisons (BMI vs waist) where an LRT cannot
- Always compare on the **same rows** (watch missing data!)
:::

# Pseudo-R² {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Three pseudo-R² measures

```{r}
r2(m_adj)                       # for logistic models r2() reports Tjur's R2
tibble(measure = c("McFadden", "Nagelkerke", "Tjur"),
       value   = c(r2_mcfadden(m_adj)$R2[[1]], r2_nagelkerke(m_adj)[[1]], r2_tjur(m_adj)[[1]])) |>
  mutate(value = round(value, 2))
```

::: {.warn}
Three **different** numbers for one model — because they are **different things**.
:::

## How to use (and not use) pseudo-R²

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.bad}
**Not**

- the same as linear R²
- "% of variance explained"
- comparable across datasets or with R² from `lm()`
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.good}
**Do**

- remember their values **run low** (a McFadden of 0.2–0.4 is already a very good fit)
- report **one** descriptively, naming it
- compare models with **LRT / AIC** instead
:::
:::
:::

## Tjur's R² has a picture

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.8
cc |> mutate(p_hat = fitted(m_adj)) |>
  ggplot(aes(htn_f, p_hat, fill = htn_f)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE, alpha = .7) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 4, shape = 18, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(col_blue, col_red)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Observed", y = "Predicted probability")
```

::: {.fragment}
Tjur's R² ≈ the **gap between the mean predicted probability** in people with and without the outcome. Handy — but still only descriptive.
:::

# Calibration and discrimination {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Two different questions

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.key}
**Calibration**

If the model says "30% risk", do **about 30%** of such people actually have hypertension?
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.key}
**Discrimination**

Does the model give **higher predicted risk to people who have** hypertension than to those who do not?
:::
:::
:::

## Calibration plot: predicted vs observed

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
cal <- cc |> mutate(p_hat = fitted(m_adj), decile = ntile(p_hat, 10)) |>
  group_by(decile) |> summarise(predicted = mean(p_hat), observed = mean(htn), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(cal, aes(predicted, observed)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = col_red) +
  geom_line(colour = col_navy) + geom_point(size = 3, colour = col_navy) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Mean predicted risk (decile of risk)", y = "Observed proportion with hypertension")
```

## Hosmer–Lemeshow test

```{r}
performance_hosmer(m_adj, n_bins = 10)
```

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.good}
**p > 0.05** → no evidence of poor calibration
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.warn}
**Limitations:** depends on the number of bins; low power in small samples, over-sensitive in huge ones; a single p-value does not show **where** the model fails. **Prefer the calibration plot.**
:::
:::
:::

## ROC curve and AUC

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
cc$p_hat <- fitted(m_adj)
roc_obj  <- roc(cc$htn, cc$p_hat, quiet = TRUE)

ggroc(roc_obj, colour = col_red, linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 1, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = .45, y = .25, size = 6, hjust = 0,
           label = paste0("AUC = ", round(auc(roc_obj), 2))) +
  labs(x = "Specificity", y = "Sensitivity")
```

## Interpreting the AUC

```{r}
auc(roc_obj)
ci.auc(roc_obj)
```

::: {.incremental}
- **AUC** = probability that a **randomly chosen hypertensive** gets a **higher predicted risk** than a **randomly chosen normotensive**
- 0.5 = coin toss · 0.7–0.8 acceptable · 0.8–0.9 good · > 0.9 excellent
- Ours: **`r round(auc(roc_obj), 2)`** (95% CI `r paste(round(ci.auc(roc_obj)[c(1,3)], 2), collapse = "–")`)
:::

## A cut-off, and a caution

```{r}
coords(roc_obj, "best", ret = c("threshold", "sensitivity", "specificity"), best.method = "youden") |> round(2)
```

::: {.incremental}
- The "best" threshold depends on purpose: **screening** (favour sensitivity) vs **confirmation** (favour specificity)
- AUC from the same data that fitted the model is **optimistic** — validate (new sample, cross-validation, bootstrap)
- Good discrimination does **not** guarantee good calibration, and vice-versa
:::

# OR vs prevalence ratio {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## The OR overstates the PR when the outcome is common

```{r}
risk <- tab$risk; or <- (risk[2] / (1 - risk[2])) / (risk[1] / (1 - risk[1])); pr <- risk[2] / risk[1]
c(prevalence_50plus = risk[2], prevalence_under50 = risk[1], PR = pr, OR = or) |> round(2)
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {.bad}
"50+ year-olds have **`r round(or, 1)` times the odds**" is true — but "**`r round(or, 1)` times as likely**" is **wrong**. They are **`r round(pr, 1)` times as likely**.
:::
:::

## Why: the gap grows with baseline risk

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4
tibble(p0 = seq(.01, .45, .005)) |>
  mutate(p1 = pmin(.99, 2 * p0), OR = (p1 / (1 - p1)) / (p0 / (1 - p0))) |>
  ggplot(aes(p0, OR)) +
  geom_line(colour = col_red, linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 2, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  annotate("text", x = .25, y = 1.6, hjust = 0, label = "dashed line = true PR of 2", size = 5) +
  labs(x = "Baseline prevalence (unexposed)", y = "OR when the true PR is 2")
```

::: {.fragment}
OR ≈ PR only when the outcome is **rare (< ~10%)**. With ~32% prevalence, the OR is far from the PR.
:::

## Getting a prevalence ratio: Poisson with robust SE

```{r}
m_pr <- glm(htn ~ age50, data = ncd, family = poisson)
m_or <- glm(htn ~ age50, data = ncd, family = binomial)
robust_vcov <- sandwich::vcovHC(m_pr, type = "HC0")

tibble(measure  = c("OR (logistic)", "PR (Poisson, robust SE)"),
       estimate = exp(c(coef(m_or)[[2]], coef(m_pr)[[2]])),
       lower    = exp(c(confint.default(m_or)[2, 1], coefci(m_pr, vcov. = robust_vcov)[2, 1])),
       upper    = exp(c(confint.default(m_or)[2, 2], coefci(m_pr, vcov. = robust_vcov)[2, 2]))) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2)))
```

::: {.incremental}
- **Poisson with robust (sandwich) SE** gives a valid PR for a binary outcome
- **Log-binomial** (`glm(family = binomial(link = "log"))`) gives the PR directly but can **fail to converge** — try it, fall back to Poisson-robust
- Adjusted PRs work the same way (add covariates)
:::

```{r}
quiz_mcq("s5q1", "Why is ordinary linear regression a poor choice for a 0/1 outcome?",
         c("It cannot include more than one predictor", "Predicted 'probabilities' can fall below 0 or above 1, and the variance is not constant",
           "It needs a larger sample size", "It only works with categorical predictors"), answer = 2,
         explain = "A straight line is unbounded and the variance of a binary outcome depends on its mean. Logistic regression models the log-odds, which is unbounded.")
```

## Self-check quiz (2/6) {.smaller}

```{r}

quiz_mcq("s5q2", "In a logistic model the coefficient for salt is β = 0.21, so e^β = 1.24. Which is the correct interpretation?",
         c("Each extra g/day of salt raises the probability of hypertension by 24 percentage points",
           "Each extra g/day of salt multiplies the odds of hypertension by 1.24, other variables held constant",
           "24% of hypertension is due to salt",
           "People eating more salt are 1.24 times as likely to be hypertensive"), answer = 2,
         explain = "exp(β) is the odds ratio for a one-unit increase: odds(x+1)/odds(x) = e^β. It is a ratio of ODDS, not of probabilities or risks.")
```

## Score and take-home

**Your score: <span class="quiz-score"></span>**

::: {.incremental}
- Logistic regression models the **log-odds**; **e^β = odds ratio**, CI limits exponentiated; **OR = 1 ⇔ β = 0**
- **Likelihood** drives assessment: compare nested models by **LRT**, others by **AIC**
- **Pseudo-R²** is descriptive, not "variance explained"
- **Calibration** (plot > Hosmer–Lemeshow) and **discrimination** (AUC) answer different questions
- For common outcomes, the **OR overstates the PR** — report the PR if you mean "times as likely"
:::
